models_evaluated: AI-driven CDSS for intravenous-to-oral antibiotic switching

links.outcome: Whether clinicians detect and ignore incorrect AI advice in vignettes
links.effect: Many decisions equivalent between SOC and CDSS arms, with clinicians able to identify and ignore incorrect advice; when differences occurred, CDSS influenced towards not switching (OR 0·13, 95% CI 0·03–0·50).
links.quote: Case vignette completion times and many decisions were equivalent between SOC and CDSS interventions, with clinicians able to identify and ignore incorrect advice.

links.outcome: Clinician decisions with versus without AI CDSS, assessing influence and reliance
links.effect: Decisions largely equivalent between arms; CDSS influenced towards not switching (χ2 7·73, p=0·0054; OR 0·13 [95% CI 0·03–0·50]); explanations used 9% of the time.
links.quote: When a statistical difference was observed, the CDSS influenced participants towards not switching (χ 2 7·73, p=0·0054; logistic regression odds ratio 0·13 [95% CI 0·03–0·50]; p=0·0031).

links.outcome: Usability (SUS, TAM) of AI CDSS among representative clinicians
links.effect: SUS 72·3/100 (SD 8·79); TAM perceived usefulness 3·6/5, ease of use 3·8/5, self-efficacy 4·1/5.
links.quote: Our software and AI CDSS obtained a good SUS score of 72·3 out of 100 (SD 8·79) and, for the TAM questionnaire, scores of 3·6 out of 5 (0·31) for perceived usefulness, 3·8 out of 5 (0·20) for perceived ease of use, and 4·1 out of 5 (0·05) for self-efficacy.

screen.practice: AI decision support with explanations versus standard information alone
screen.reason: The study conducts a randomized clinical vignette experiment evaluating the impact of an AI clinical decision support system (with explanations) on clinicians' prescribing decisions compared to standard of care.

primary.practice: AI-driven CDSS with explanations vs standard of care
